name: eprover
desc: Theorem prover for full first-order logic with equality
why: A serious first-order logic theorem prover you can drive from the terminal, a real window into automated reasoning.

brief.what_it_is: E is an automated theorem prover, written in C and distributed under the GNU GPL, for many-sorted first-order logic with equality. The README says it can also take polymorphic higher-order logic when built with --enable-ho. You feed it a problem file, a specification plus a conjecture, in formats it detects automatically (LOP, TPTP-2 or TPTP-3). It runs a search and, if it succeeds, reports a proof, optionally in a proof-object format that the bundled checkproof tool can verify. The package also ships helper programs for strategy scheduling, parallel runs, proof filtering, and a knowledge-base (ekb_*) toolset.
brief.why_it_exists: The README frames E as an equational theorem prover for stating a mathematical specification and a conjecture and letting the machine search for a proof. It is candid that this can run for a long time: 'which will then run forever, using up all of your machines resources. Very occasionally it will find a proof for the conjecture and tell you so ;-).'
brief.how_it_works: By default the prover runs a single strategy, or with --auto it picks a heuristic strategy based on the problem, pruning the axiom set for large inputs, which the README says may cost completeness. The --satauto variant keeps completeness. The --auto-schedule modes run a series of strategies in sequence, assuming a 300-second budget unless --cpu-limit says otherwise, and --auto-schedule=n spreads them across n cores. Proof objects can be written out and checked with checkproof.

brief.install_notes: Requires GNU tar, sh and gawk on the search path, per the README's quick-install section. Standard path: unpack E.tgz, cd E, run ./configure (optionally with --bindir=EXECDIR), then make and make install, which needs write permission to EXECDIR (sudo if outside your home). Alternatively build in place with ./configure, make rebuild, then run from the PROVER directory. Higher-order support needs --enable-ho and produces eprover-ho. Building the manual needs LaTeX2e, pdflatex, and the theorem, amssymb and epsfig packages, though a precompiled DOC/eprover.pdf is also included. For non-GNU compilers, the README points to editing Makefile.vars and to DOC/PORTING. No accounts or runtimes beyond a C toolchain and the shell utilities are mentioned.
brief.standout: It is a long-running, research-grade prover with a strategy-scheduling layer that tries many strategies in sequence or across cores, rather than a single search. It also has a proof-object format plus an independent checker (checkproof), so a claimed proof can be verified separately.
brief.status: Maintained, as far as the README shows. It is labelled version 3.5 'Countess Grey', credited to Stephan Schulz with several contributors, and the README says the canonical source is README.md. I could not see a release date or last-commit date in the fetched text, so recent activity is unconfirmed. The homepage returned no content, so I could not check its news or release notes.
brief.caveats: The homepage https://eprover.org/ returned an empty response, so this brief relies on the GitHub README alone. The brew description says first-order logic with equality, but higher-order support needs a separate build with --enable-ho. Auto mode may be incomplete on very large axiom sets, and checkproof cannot check the full first-order part. The README asks that bug reports go by email to the maintainer, and it notes that this is an unpaid volunteer service. Licence is GPL, which the README says comes with no warranty. The scout note's 'real window into automated reasoning' is an editorial phrase, not from the project.

entry.title: E (eprover)
entry.tldr: A research-grade automated theorem prover: give it axioms and a conjecture in first-order logic, and it searches for a proof.
entry.deeper_look:
E is an automated theorem prover for many-sorted first-order logic with equality, written in C. You write a problem file containing a specification (axioms) and a conjecture, in LOP, TPTP-2 or TPTP-3 format, which it detects on its own. E then searches for a proof. If it finds one, it prints it. If it does not, it may keep going for a very long time.

The README is candid about this. It says the prover will "run forever, using up all of your machines resources. Very occasionally it will find a proof for the conjecture and tell you so ;-)." Automated reasoning is a hard search problem, and E treats it that way: with `--auto` it picks a heuristic strategy based on the problem, and with `--auto-schedule` it runs a series of strategies in turn, assuming a 300-second budget unless told otherwise. `--auto-schedule=n` spreads those strategies across n cores.

The idea underneath is that a proof can be found by machine and then checked separately. E can write proof objects, and the bundled `checkproof` tool verifies them, though it skips the non-clausal parts. The package also ships helpers for strategy parameter search, axiom filtering, and a knowledge-base toolset (the `ekb_*` programs). Higher-order logic is possible only if E is built with `--enable-ho`, which the brew formula's description does not claim.

try_this.what_happens: Prints usage information and the long list of options, a quick look at how many knobs a prover has.
Runs automatic strategy selection on your problem file and prints a proof object if it finds one.
Tries a schedule of strategies spread across 8 CPU cores, usually stronger than a single automatic strategy.

entry.whats_unique: E has a strategy-scheduling layer that tries many search strategies in sequence or across cores, rather than betting on one. It also pairs its proofs with an independent checker, so a claimed proof can be verified separately.
entry.caveats: You must write or find your own problem files (TPTP is the usual source), auto mode may lose completeness on very large axiom sets, and the homepage returned nothing when checked, so the GitHub README is the main reference.
